The earlier sections built models and scored them on new sites. A score says how well a
model predicts; a study also has to say what the model found, how sure the finding is,
and how far it reaches. This section takes that last step, on the same simulated survey
as the rest of the course.
The first two pages read a black box from outside:

- **feature importance**: shuffling one input on test sites shows how much a random
  forest relies on it, and columns of random numbers show what an unused input scores;
  the forest's own measure ranked them above the seabed;
- **partial effects**: a partial dependence plot draws how a prediction changes along
  one input, and ICE curves draw it station by station; the forest finds the
  temperature hump at nearly every station, while its depth curve follows position.

The next two read a model from its parts and say how sure its predictions are:

- **black boxes and interpretable models**: scored on the same folds of sites, a GAM
  predicts new sites as well as a random forest, and its curves and multipliers read
  as a habitat description; a black box earns its place where inputs work in
  combination;
- **communicating uncertainty**: an interval for the average and an interval for a new
  catch answer different questions, and conformal prediction gives any model an
  interval that holds at stations like the ones that set it.

The last two turn the analysis into a report:

- **reproducibility and transparent reporting**: a seed makes a run repeat, but the
  split of sites moves a forest's score far more than its seed, and a short report
  lets a reader re-run the whole analysis;
- **from a model to a claim**: the Methods and Results paragraphs are written from the
  code, the simulation confirms the temperature curve but not a depth peak, and a gear
  that misses animals on rock improves the cross-validated score.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones.
[Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) built
the forest that [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) and
[Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd) read from outside.
[Linearity and nonlinearity](../06-assumptions-limitations/linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd)
fitted the GAM and found its depth curve wrong; [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd)
shows why no model gets it right on this survey, and
[Black boxes and interpretable models](black-box-or-not.qmd) reads the GAM's parts with
the multipliers of
[Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd).
[Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd)
gave the forest intervals from a quantile forest, and
[Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) put an
interval on a score; [Communicating uncertainty](communicating-uncertainty.qmd) checks
intervals on predictions by their coverage at new sites.
[Checking a fit](../04-how-algorithms-learn/reading-a-fit.qmd) measured how far a forest
moves without a seed; [Reproducibility and transparent reporting](reproducibility.qmd)
compares that with the split of sites.
[Exploring the data first](../02-marine-data/exploratory-analysis.qmd) compared records
by gear, and [From a model to a claim](from-model-to-claim.qmd) shows
the bias that no comparison of a model with its records can find.

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [Explaining models and predictions](https://www.tmwr.org/explain.html), Tidy Modeling with R. Local and global explanations through `DALEX`, in tidymodels idiom.
- [DALEX](https://modeloriented.github.io/DALEX/), Przemyslaw Biecek and others. Model-agnostic explanation for R and Python both.
- [Permutation importance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance.html) and [partial dependence and ICE](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/partial_dependence.html), scikit-learn user guide. The permutation page shows what inputs that move together do to the scores.
- [Interpretable Machine Learning](https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/), Christoph Molnar. A free book, and the standard reference for every method named here.
